problem: The definition 'A heart sound is a short vibration set off when a valve closes' is contradicted two sentences later, where S3 and S4 are described as sounds made by blood moving into the ventricle, not by valve closure. A student learns a definition that then fails for two of the four sounds the chapter names.
fix: Most heart sounds come from a valve shutting; S3 and S4 instead come from the way blood moves into the ventricles during filling. Say: 'A heart sound is a short vibration from the heart and great vessels. S1 and S2 come from a valve closing; S3 and S4 come from blood entering the ventricle.'

problem: 'S3 and S4 are common in young people and are not always disease' lumps the two together. S3 is a normal finding in children and young adults, but S4 is normal mainly in children and trained athletes; in an older adult it usually points to a stiff, poorly compliant ventricle and is a sign of disease.
fix: 'S3 is common in children and young adults and is often harmless. S4 can be normal in children and athletes, but in an older adult it usually means a stiff ventricle and suggests disease.'

problem: The claim that murmurs 'carry more high-frequency energy than normal S1 and S2' is too broad and sits badly with the same chapter's own example of a low-pitched mitral stenosis murmur that needs the bell. A student may conclude every murmur is high frequency and reach for the diaphragm every time.
fix: 'Turbulent flow adds higher frequencies than the low rumble of S3 and S4, but murmurs vary: aortic stenosis and regurgitation are relatively high-pitched, while mitral stenosis is low-pitched and needs the bell.'

problem: 'S1 and S2 follow it by fixed delays' overstates the case. The delay from the R wave to S1 is short and fairly stable, but the R-to-S2 delay changes with heart rate, contractility and conduction, which is exactly why the delays must be measured on each trace.
fix: 'S1 and S2 follow the R wave by short, repeatable delays that are measured on each trace; the S2 delay in particular lengthens as the heart rate falls.'
